setup: A portfolio holds five positions of USD 2 million each. Every position has return volatility $\sigma = 30\%$ and every pair is correlated at $\rho = 0.2$. Use $z = 2.33$ and $\sigma_P = \sigma\sqrt{1/N + (1 - 1/N)\rho}$.
ask: Portfolio VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.84m
options.why: Used one USD 2m position as the portfolio value. Five positions of USD 2m is a USD 10m portfolio.

options.label: ≈ USD 13m
options.why: Scale slip (3×). Even with no diversification at all ($\sigma_P = 30\%$) VaR is only $2.33 \times 0.30 \times 10 = \text{USD } 7.0\text{m}$, so the answer must sit below that.

options.label: ≈ USD 42m
options.why: Scale slip (10×). The undiversified ceiling is USD 7.0m; nothing with $\rho < 1$ can exceed it.

takeaway: Equal-weight VaR sits between the large-$N$ floor $z\sigma\sqrt{\rho}\,P$ and the undiversified ceiling $z\sigma P$, and $P$ is the whole portfolio, not one position.

setup: Portfolio X has a VaR of EUR 400,000 and holds four equally weighted assets of EUR 1,000,000 each. Asset A has a beta of 1.2 against the portfolio.
ask: Asset A's marginal VaR (change in portfolio VaR per extra euro in A) is closest to:

options.why: Also multiplied by A's 25% weight. $\text{MVaR}_A \times w_A$ is A's component VaR per euro of portfolio, not the per-euro marginal VaR.
Divided by one asset's EUR 1m instead of the EUR 4m portfolio.
Never divided by portfolio value. $400{,}000 \times 1.2$ is a euro amount, not a per-euro sensitivity.

takeaway: Marginal VaR is a per-dollar number, $(\text{VaR}_P / P) \times \beta_i$. It sits near 0.1, not in the thousands.

setup: Assets A and B are uncorrelated: volatilities 6% and 14%, positions USD 4m and USD 2m. Per-dollar covariances with the portfolio are $\text{cov}(R_A, R_P) = 0.0144$ and $\text{cov}(R_B, R_P) = 0.0392$, and the portfolio's dollar variance is $0.136$ (in USD m$^2$). Use $z = 1.65$.
ask: The rise in VaR from adding USD 10,000 to asset A is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 190
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). $\text{MVaR}_A \approx 0.064$ per dollar, so a USD 10,000 add moves VaR by several hundred dollars.

options.label: ≈ USD 1,800
options.why: Used asset B's marginal VaR (0.175). The trade size is right but the asset is wrong.

options.label: ≈ USD 260,000
options.why: Multiplied A's marginal VaR by its whole USD 4m position. That is A's component VaR, not the effect of a USD 10,000 add.

takeaway: For a small trade, incremental VaR ≈ marginal VaR × trade size. On a USD 10k add that is hundreds of dollars, not the whole position.

setup: Assets A and B are uncorrelated: A (6% vol, USD 4m) and B (14% vol, USD 2m). You have the per-dollar covariances with the portfolio, $\text{cov}(R_A, R_P) = 0.0144$ and $\text{cov}(R_B, R_P) = 0.0392$. Both marginal VaRs share the same factor $z / \sigma_P$.
ask: Which asset has the larger marginal VaR, and so is the one to trim to cut VaR fastest?

options.label: A, because its position is twice as large
options.why: Position size does not decide it. MVaR is proportional to $\text{cov}(R_i, R_P)$, and B's 0.0392 is 2.7× A's 0.0144 despite the smaller position.

options.label: Neither: uncorrelated assets have equal marginal VaRs
options.why: Zero correlation between A and B does not equalise their covariance with the portfolio. Each still covaries with the portfolio through its own $\sigma_i^2 x_i$.

takeaway: To cut VaR fastest, trim the position with the highest marginal VaR. Here that is the smaller but more volatile B.

setup: A CAD 248m portfolio (volatility 16%) holds CAD 15m of stock T (volatility 13%). The correlation between T and the portfolio is 0.45. Use a 1-year 95% VaR with $z = 1.645$.
ask: The component VaR of stock T is closest to:

options.label: ≈ CAD 0.096m
options.why: Dropped the position size. $1.645 \times 0.13 \times 0.45$ is per CAD 1 of T, not for the CAD 15m holding.

options.label: ≈ CAD 3.9m
options.why: Two slips: T's individual VaR computed with the portfolio's 16% volatility instead of T's 13%, and never multiplied by the correlation.

options.label: ≈ CAD 29m
options.why: Applied the correlation to the whole portfolio's VaR, $1.645 \times 0.16 \times 248 \times 0.45$. The CAD 248m is a red herring.

takeaway: Component VaR = individual VaR × correlation with the portfolio. The portfolio's size never enters.

setup: Stock T is a CAD 15m holding (volatility 13%) in a larger portfolio. You've computed its 95% individual VaR: $\text{VaR}_T = 15 \times 0.13 \times 1.645 = \text{CAD } 3.21\text{m}$. T's correlation with the portfolio is 0.45.
ask: T's component VaR is above CAD 3.21m, below it, or equal to it?

options.label: Above CAD 3.21m
options.why: Component VaR is $\text{VaR}_T \times \rho$ and $\rho \le 1$, so it can never exceed the stand-alone figure.

options.label: Equal to CAD 3.21m
options.why: This is the classic intermediate-result slip: stopping at the individual VaR. The two are equal only at ρ = 1.

takeaway: Component VaR ≤ individual VaR. With ρ = 0.45 it is under half.

setup: A portfolio holds USD 8m in asset A and USD 4m in asset B. Daily volatilities are 1.5% and 2.0%, and the correlation is 0.6. Use $z = 2.33$ (99%) and a 10-day horizon.
ask: The 10-day 99% VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.42m
options.why: Forgot the $\sqrt{10}$. That is the 1-day VaR.

options.label: ≈ USD 4.2m
options.why: Scaled by 10 instead of $\sqrt{10}$. Variance scales with time; volatility scales with its square root.

options.label: ≈ USD 16m
options.why: Multiplied the dollar σ, which is already in USD m, by the USD 12m portfolio value again.

takeaway: Scale VaR by $\sqrt{t}$. A σ built from dollar positions is already in dollars, so don't multiply by portfolio value again.

setup: A portfolio holds two long positions: USD 8m in A (1.5% daily vol) and USD 4m in B (2.0% daily vol), correlated at 0.6, with a 10-day 99% VaR of USD 1.32m. The correlation rises to 0.9. Positions and volatilities are unchanged.
ask: The 10-day VaR:

options.label: Falls
options.why: Higher correlation means less diversification. The cross term $2x_Ax_B\rho\sigma_A\sigma_B$ grows with ρ when both positions are long.

options.label: Stays roughly the same
options.why: The cross term rises from 0.0115 to 0.0173, lifting VaR from USD 1.32m to about USD 1.44m, a rise of roughly 9%.

takeaway: With both positions long, correlation up → diversification down → VaR up.

setup: A USD 3m portfolio holds CAD (66.67%) and EUR (33.33%) currency positions. Marginal VaRs are 0.0528 for CAD and 0.1521 for EUR. You want the lowest possible VaR with the full USD 3m still invested.
ask: Which way should the mix shift?

options.label: Cut CAD, add EUR
options.why: Backwards. Cut the position with the highest marginal VaR (EUR, 0.1521) and add to the one with the lowest (CAD, 0.0528).

options.label: Leave it: the mix is already minimum-risk
options.why: At the global minimum all marginal VaRs are equal. 0.0528 and 0.1521 are far apart.

takeaway: Minimum risk means all marginal VaRs are equal, so move money from the high-MVaR position to the low-MVaR one.

setup: A USD 3m portfolio holds CAD (66.67%) and EUR (33.33%). Excess expected returns are 8% for CAD and 5% for EUR. Betas against the portfolio are 0.615 for CAD and 1.770 for EUR. The return-optimal portfolio equalises $E_i / \beta_i$ across assets.
ask: Right now, which ratio $E_i / \beta_i$ is larger?

options.label: EUR's
options.why: EUR has the lower return and the higher beta, and both push its ratio down: 0.05 / 1.770 = 0.028 against CAD's 0.130.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: 0.130 against 0.028 is more than four times apart.

working.label: Action
working.display: Add to CAD: the optimum is at 90.21% CAD, where both ratios equal 0.0771

takeaway: For the optimal portfolio, add to the asset with the highest excess return per unit of beta (or marginal VaR). Here that is CAD.

setup: Two managers start from the same CAD/EUR portfolio (volatility 15.62%; excess returns 8% CAD, 5% EUR). Manager 1 rebalances to the minimum-risk mix. Manager 2 rebalances to the mix that maximises excess return per unit of VaR.
ask: Compared with Manager 1's portfolio, Manager 2's volatility is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Nothing can have lower volatility than the minimum-risk portfolio. That is its definition.

options.label: Identical: both equalise marginal VaRs
options.why: Only the minimum-risk portfolio equalises marginal VaRs. The optimum equalises $E_i / \text{MVaR}_i$, which tilts further into CAD (90.21% against 85.21%) and lands at 13.98% against 13.85%.

working.label: Difference
working.display: $13.98 - 13.85 = +0.13$ pts, bought with a Sharpe ratio of 0.551 against 0.546

takeaway: Minimum-risk is not optimal. Adding return to the objective accepts a little more risk.

setup: Two-currency portfolio: USD 2m CAD and USD 1m EUR, VaR USD 257.7k. EUR's marginal VaR is 0.1521, so its component VaR is $0.1521 \times 1{,}000{,}000 = \text{USD } 152.1\text{k}$. A full revaluation with the EUR position removed gives a VaR of USD 165.0k.
ask: The actual VaR reduction from dropping EUR, compared with EUR's component VaR, is:

options.label: Larger
options.why: 257.7 − 165.0 = 92.7k, well under 152.1k. VaR is convex in the position, so the curve stays above its tangent and the tangent overstates the drop.

options.label: About the same, since component VaR measures exactly this
options.why: Component VaR is only a linear approximation. It works for small positions and poorly for one that is a third of the portfolio: here the gap is about USD 60k.

takeaway: Component VaR travels down the tangent and incremental VaR down the curve. For a large position they differ a lot.

setup: A candidate answer for the return-optimal CAD/EUR portfolio quotes weights of 90.21% CAD and 9.79% EUR, with betas against the portfolio of 1.038 (CAD) and 0.649 (EUR).
ask: Its weighted-average beta is above 1, below 1, or equal to 1 (to rounding)?

options.label: Above 1: CAD's beta exceeds 1 and CAD dominates
Below 1: EUR's beta has dropped to 0.649
options.why: EUR's low beta carries only a 9.79% weight. The total is $0.936 + 0.064 = 1.000$.

takeaway: Betas measured against the portfolio itself always average to exactly 1. That gives a free check on any candidate answer.

setup: The average Dow stock correlation this month is 30%; its long-run mean is 35%. A regression of the monthly change in correlation on its level gives $Y = 0.273 - 0.78X$.
ask: Next month's expected correlation is:

options.label: Below 30%
options.why: Took the slope's sign at face value (a = −0.78). The mean-reversion rate is minus the slope, a = +0.78, which pulls correlation up toward 35%.

options.label: Above 35%
options.why: With 0 < a < 1 the variable closes only part of the gap (78% of 5 points). It would overshoot the mean only if a > 1.

takeaway: Regression slope = −a. With 0 < a < 1, the next value lands between today's level and the mean.

setup: Correlation was 0.22 a year ago and is 0.35 now; its long-run mean is 0.45. The implied mean-reversion rate is $a = (S_t - S_{t-1}) / (\mu - S_{t-1})$.
ask: Is the implied mean-reversion rate above 50%, below 50%, or too close to call?

options.label: Below 50%
options.why: Divided the move by the mean (0.13 / 0.45 = 0.29) instead of by the starting gap $\mu - S_{t-1} = 0.23$.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: Half the starting gap is 0.115 and the move is 0.13, clearly more than half (a ≈ 56.5%).

takeaway: a is the fraction of the gap closed. Compare the move with half of $\mu - S_{t-1}$.

setup: Dow stock correlations show a one-period mean-reversion rate of 78%. A later sample shows the mean-reversion rate rising to 90%.
ask: The one-period-lag autocorrelation of those correlations:

options.label: Rises
options.why: The reverse property: autocorrelation = 1 − mean-reversion rate, so it goes from 0.22 to 0.10.

options.label: Is unchanged, because they measure different things
options.why: For the one-period lag they are complements that always sum to 1.

takeaway: Mean reversion and one-lag autocorrelation sum to 1: more of one means less of the other.

setup: In the 1972–2012 Dow study, the average equity correlation rises steadily from expansion (27%) to normal periods (33%) to recessions (37%).
ask: Moving from a normal period into recession, correlation volatility:

options.label: Falls slightly, staying above its expansion level
Rises to its highest level
options.why: Tempting because the correlation level rises, but correlation volatility peaked in the normal period (83.06%) and dipped to 80.48% in recession.

options.label: Falls to its lowest level of the three states
options.why: The lowest volatility (71.17%) is in expansions. Recession's 80.48% is only a little below the normal period's 83.06%.

working.label: Change
working.display: $80.48 - 83.06 = -2.58$ pts; expansion is lower still at $71.17\%$

takeaway: Correlation level peaks in recessions; correlation volatility peaks in normal times.

setup: A 99% one-day VaR model is backtested over 252 trading days and records 6 exceptions.
ask: Relative to its target, the model is:

options.label: Overestimating risk
options.why: The failure rate, 6/252 = 2.38%, is above the 1% target. Too many exceptions means VaR is set too low, so risk is understated.

options.label: About right
options.why: About 2.5 exceptions are expected; 6 is more than double that.

takeaway: Too many exceptions means VaR is too low and risk is underestimated. Too few means capital is over-allocated.

setup: A 95% daily VaR is backtested over $T = 252$ days and breached on 20 of them. Use the normal approximation $z = (x - pT)/\sqrt{p(1-p)T}$.
ask: The test statistic z is closest to:

options.why: Divided by the variance $p(1-p)T = 11.97$ instead of its square root.
Stopped at the excess count $x - pT$ and never standardised it.
Scale slip (10×). The excess is 7.4 exceptions and the standard error about 3.5, so z is a single digit.

takeaway: z is excess exceptions divided by their standard error, so it comes out in single digits. Compare it with 1.96.

setup: A 95% daily VaR backtest shows 20 exceptions in 252 days at $p = 0.05$. You have the excess $x - pT = 7.4$ and the standard error $\sqrt{0.05 \times 0.95 \times 252} = 3.46$. The two-tailed 5% critical value is 1.96.
ask: Is $7.4 - 1.96 \times 3.46$ positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Negative, so accept the model
options.why: 1.96 × 3.46 = 6.78, which is below 7.4. Equivalently z = 2.14 > 1.96.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The margin is about 0.6 exceptions, and z = 2.14 against 1.96 is a clear, if modest, rejection.

takeaway: Rejection needs more than about 2 standard errors of excess exceptions. Here 7.4 > 6.8, so reject.

setup: Basel backtest: a 99% VaR model checked over the last 250 trading days records 7 exceptions. The base capital multiplier is 3.
ask: The capital multiplier:

options.label: Stays at 3
options.why: The green zone is 0 to 4 exceptions; 7 falls in the yellow zone.

options.label: Jumps to 4
options.why: The red zone, with multiplier 4, starts at 10 exceptions.

working.label: Zone
working.display: 7 exceptions → yellow (5 to 9): multiplier between 3 and 4

takeaway: Basel zones: 0 to 4 green (multiplier 3), 5 to 9 yellow (3 to 4), 10 or more red (4). Expected is 2.5.

setup: A credit line has a USD 10m limit with USD 4m drawn. Behavioural modelling puts the chance the rest is drawn at 60%. Funding the liquidity cushion costs 18 bp.
ask: The charge for contingent liquidity risk is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 1.9 bp
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). The charge is 36% of the 18 bp cushion cost, so it is about 6 to 7 bp.

options.label: ≈ 18 bp
options.why: Charged the full cushion cost, skipping both the undrawn proportion (0.60) and the drawdown likelihood (0.60).

options.label: ≈ 650 bp
options.why: Decimal slip: treated 18 bp as 0.18 (18%) instead of 0.0018.

takeaway: Contingent charge = undrawn share × drawdown likelihood × cushion cost, which is always a fraction of the cushion cost.

setup: A credit line has a USD 10m limit, 60% drawdown likelihood, 18 bp cushion cost. The customer draws a further USD 2m, taking the drawn amount from USD 4m to USD 6m.
ask: The contingent liquidity charge on the line:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Only the undrawn part is contingent. The drawn USD 6m carries its own on-balance-sheet FTP charge. The undrawn share falls from 0.60 to 0.40, so the charge goes from 6.48 to 4.32 bp.

options.label: Is unchanged, since the limit is the same
options.why: The charge scales with the undrawn proportion of the limit, not with the limit itself.

takeaway: A drawdown moves exposure from contingent to funded: the contingent charge falls while the loan picks up its own FTP charge.

setup: A bank prices liquidity with a single pooled average cost of funds across all funding sources and maturities. A business unit books a 10-year fixed-rate loan.
ask: Relative to its true liquidity cost, the 10-year loan is charged:

options.label: Too much
options.why: The pooled average sits below the true cost of long-term funding, so long assets are undercharged and short assets overcharged.

options.label: About right, since averaging is unbiased
options.why: Averaging ignores maturity. It is only right for an asset whose maturity happens to match the average; a 10-year loan is at the long end.

working.label: Pooled average vs long funding
working.display: The single average cost < the marginal cost of 10-year funding

takeaway: Pooled average cost undercharges long-term assets and overcharges short-term ones.

setup: A 3-year CDS on a reference entity with a hazard rate of 3% per year and a recovery rate of 35%. The risk-free rate is 4% (continuous). Premiums are paid annually; defaults are assumed mid-year, with accrued premium paid on default.
ask: The breakeven CDS spread is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 2 bp
options.why: Units slip: 0.0199 is 1.99%, which is 199 bp, not 1.99 bp.

options.label: ≈ 60 bp
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). Sanity anchor: spread ≈ hazard × (1 − R) = 3% × 0.65 ≈ 195 bp.

options.label: ≈ 530 bp
options.why: Took the PV of the payoff leg (0.0528) as the spread and never divided by the premium annuity $A + B = 2.65$.

takeaway: Sanity anchor for any CDS spread: $s \approx \lambda(1 - R)$, here about 195 bp.

setup: A 3-year CDS (hazard 3%, recovery 35%, risk-free 4%). Per unit of spread, the PV of expected premium payments is $A = 2.6123$ and the PV of accrued premium on default is $B = 0.0406$. The PV of the expected payoff is $C = 0.0528$, and $s = C/(A + B)$.
ask: If you forget $B$, the spread you compute is higher, lower, or the same to the nearest bp?

options.label: Lower
options.why: Dropping B shrinks the denominator, so s rises: 0.0528 / 2.6123 = 202 bp against 199 bp.

options.label: The same to the nearest bp
options.why: B is small but not negligible. It moves the spread by about 3 bp.

takeaway: Forgetting the accrual leg credits the buyer with less value paid in, so the breakeven spread comes out too high.

setup: A reference entity (hazard 3%, recovery 35%, 3 years), where a regular CDS breaks even at about 199 bp. A binary CDS on it pays the full notional on default, whatever the recovery.
ask: The binary CDS's breakeven spread, compared with the regular one, is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: The payoff per default rises from $1 - R = 0.65$ to 1, so C and the spread both rise by a factor of 1/0.65, to about 306 bp.

options.label: The same, because default probabilities haven't changed
options.why: The premium leg is unchanged but the payoff leg is bigger, and spread = PV of payoff / annuity.

takeaway: A binary CDS's payoff is not reduced by recovery, so its protection costs more.

setup: The 5-year CDX NA IG index (125 names) is quoted at 66 bp. A trader buys USD 800,000 of protection on each name.
ask: The annual protection cost is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 5,300
options.why: Priced one name only and forgot the ×125. (This is also how much the annual payment drops after one default.)

options.label: ≈ USD 6.6m
options.why: Read 66 bp as 0.066 (6.6%) instead of 0.0066.

options.label: ≈ USD 66m
options.why: Read 66 bp as 0.66.

takeaway: Index cost = spread × notional per name × 125, and 1 bp is 1/10,000.

setup: You bought 5-year CDS protection a year ago. Since then the reference entity's CDS spread has narrowed substantially, and no credit event has occurred.
ask: The mark-to-market value of your position as protection buyer:

options.label: Is positive: you have gained
options.why: Narrower spreads mean protection is now cheaper than the rate you locked in. The seller's MtM (PV of premiums − PV of payoff) is positive, so the buyer's is negative.

options.label: Is zero until a credit event occurs
options.why: A CDS is marked to market as spreads move, not only on default.

working.label: Buyer's MtM
working.display: The negative of the seller's: a loss

takeaway: When spreads narrow, the protection seller gains and the buyer loses. When they widen, the reverse.

setup: A bank has USD 100m of retail exposures, 1-year PD 2%, recovery 60%, copula correlation 0.1. Use $N^{-1}(0.02) = -2.054$ and $N^{-1}(0.999) = 3.090$, with $\text{WCDR} = N\!\left[\dfrac{N^{-1}(\text{PD}) + \sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right]$.
ask: The one-year 99.9% credit VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.028m
options.why: Sign slip: subtracted the factor term $\sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)$, which gives a WCDR (about 0.07%) below the PD itself.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.80m
options.why: Used the average PD (2%) instead of the worst-case default rate. That is expected loss, not VaR.

options.label: ≈ USD 15m
options.why: Scale slip (3×). Even with zero recovery the loss would be 100 × 0.128 = USD 12.8m, so the VaR can't exceed that.

takeaway: Credit VaR uses the worst-case default rate, not the PD. Here the WCDR is about 12.8% against a PD of 2%.

setup: A retail book: PD 2%, $\rho = 0.1$, 99.9% confidence. You have $N^{-1}(0.02) = -2.0537$ and $\sqrt{0.1} \times N^{-1}(0.999) = 0.3162 \times 3.0902$.
ask: The WCDR numerator $N^{-1}(\text{PD}) + \sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)$ is positive, negative, or near zero?

options.label: Positive
options.why: The factor term is only 0.977, not enough to offset −2.054. The numerator is −1.077.

options.label: Near zero
options.why: −1.08 is not near zero. It maps to a WCDR of about 12.8%, well below 50%.

takeaway: A negative numerator means a WCDR below 50%. The stress lifts a 2% PD to about 13%, not to a coin flip.

setup: One-factor Gaussian copula: $Q(T \mid F) = N\!\left(\dfrac{N^{-1}[Q(T)] - \sqrt{\rho}\,F}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)$ with $Q(T) = 2\%$ ($N^{-1} = -2.054$) and $\rho = 0.1$. The common factor realisation $F$ moves from 0 to −2.
ask: The conditional default probability $Q(T \mid F)$:

options.label: Falls
options.why: F enters with a minus sign. A lower F raises the argument of N, so the conditional PD rises. Low F is the bad state of the world.

options.label: Is unchanged, because only ρ matters
options.why: F enters the formula directly. ρ sets how strongly it bites.

takeaway: In $Q(T \mid F)$, F enters negatively: bad factor draws (low F) raise conditional PDs.

setup: A bank has a derivatives book with one counterparty. The bank's own credit quality deteriorates; the counterparty's is unchanged, and so is the no-default value of the trades. Some of the trades could end up with the bank owing money to the counterparty.
ask: The credit-adjusted value of the book to the bank:

options.label: Falls
options.why: The bank's own default risk feeds DVA, which is added: a higher bank PD means a higher DVA and a higher value to the bank.

options.label: Is unchanged, because only counterparty risk (CVA) matters
options.why: DVA captures the bank's own default and is added to the no-default value.

working.label: Effect
working.display: Bank PD up → $q_i^*$ up → DVA up → value up

takeaway: CVA (counterparty default) is subtracted and DVA (own default) is added, so a worsening in your own credit raises the book's value to you.
